title: FPT Status of Single-Machine Scheduling with Forbidden Start and End Times
short_statement: FPT is proved for integer-time forbidden start-and-end instants; the recorded formulation omitted the time-domain restriction.
open_problem: Historical target: classify FPT in the number of forbidden start/end instants. The integer-time interpretation is solved; reconcile any intended nonintegral data or real-time schedules explicitly before extending that conclusion.
background: Forbidden endpoints model auxiliary resources needed to initiate or complete jobs; processing can continue across forbidden instants. Earlier XP bounds motivated parameterized questions. The prior record understated the high-multiplicity Fse result and did not distinguish its integer-time assumptions from unspecified real-time schedules. Forbidden-start-only (Fs) and forbidden-start-and-end (Fse) results also require separate treatment.
full_statement: Consider a single machine and a set of nonpreemptive jobs with processing times. There is also a set $F$ of $\tau$ forbidden time points. A feasible schedule processes one job at a time and must avoid starting or completing any job at a forbidden time point; equivalently, every job start time and completion time must lie outside $F$. The objective is to minimize the makespan. The original target is an algorithm with running time $f(\tau)L^{O(1)}$, where $L$ is the encoded input length, or a parameterized hardness classification. The record did not specify the time domain. Gabay, Rapine, and Brauner's Theorem 3 proves FPT for integer data and integer start/completion times, including high-multiplicity encoding. This settles that discrete-time interpretation, not unrestricted real-time schedules without a reduction or discretization argument. The original target is retained with this scope caveat.
known_results: Gabay, Rapine, and Brauner, Journal of Scheduling 19(5), 609-616 (2016), Theorem 3, proves FPT in the number of forbidden start-and-end instants even with high multiplicities. The model requires integer data and integer feasible endpoints. The previous XP-only description is incorrect for that model. Billaut-Sourd concerns forbidden starts; Rapine-Brauner concerns forbidden starts and completions. No conclusion about an unspecified real-time interpretation follows without additional argument.

progress.summary: The discrete-time Fse interpretation is resolved; omitted time-domain assumptions prevent an unqualified resolved label.

counterexample_rationale: Finite schedules can test implementations and modeling assumptions; a purported hardness result must not contradict the published discrete-time classification without addressing that theorem.
alphaevolve_rationale: Computation can validate small schedules and discretization claims, not rediscover the already proved integer-time FPT result.

literature.synthesis: The integer-time Fse theorem supersedes the XP-only summary. The remaining issue in this record is precise model reconciliation, not evidence that a distinct real-time problem is currently open.

agent_guidance.suitable_approaches: Fix the input encoding and allowed time domain first. Use the published algorithm for integer-time Fse; supply an explicit reduction for any other interpretation.
agent_guidance.verification_notes: Check integer data and integer feasible endpoints, nonpreemption, forbidden starts AND completions, makespan objective, and encoded input length. Scaling rational data alone does not prove integer schedules suffice. Real-time formulations must address attainment of the objective.

where_posed.text: Historical survey pointer retained from the original record. Its exact formulation should not be conflated with the integer-time Fse theorem; this audit does not certify that Open Problem 4 poses the identical model.
